stories.title: The 1948 war
stories.teaser: How partition, war and flight created Israel and the Palestinian refugee question.
stories.summary: The war began as a civil war between Jewish and Arab communities in British-ruled Palestine after the UN voted for partition in November 1947. It became a war between Israel and neighbouring Arab states after Israel declared independence in May 1948. It ended with the 1949 armistice agreements, with Israel holding more territory than the UN plan had allotted to the Jewish state, and with around 700,000 Palestinian Arabs displaced.

background.t: Under the British Mandate (1920–1948), Jewish immigration and land purchase, and the growth of both Zionist and Palestinian Arab nationalism, produced recurring violence, including the Arab revolt of 1936–39.
On 29 November 1947 the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 181, recommending partition into a Jewish state and an Arab state, with an international regime for Jerusalem.
The Jewish Agency accepted the partition plan. The Arab Higher Committee and the Arab states rejected it.

course.t: Fighting between Jewish and Palestinian Arab forces began immediately after the vote and lasted until May 1948, while Britain prepared to leave.
Israel declared independence on 14 May 1948. From 15 May, armies from Egypt, Transjordan, Syria and Iraq, and a smaller Lebanese force, entered the former Mandate territory.
Two UN truces interrupted the fighting in June–July 1948. Israeli offensives in the second half of 1948 enlarged the area under Israeli control.

outcome.t: Israel signed armistice agreements with Egypt (24 February 1949), Lebanon (23 March), Jordan (3 April) and Syria (20 July). The armistice lines, later called the Green Line, became Israel's de facto borders until 1967.
Jordan took control of the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and annexed it in 1950. Egypt administered the Gaza Strip.

Around 700,000 Palestinian Arabs fled or were expelled from the territory that became Israel. Contemporary estimates range from about 540,000 to over 900,000. The UN Conciliation Commission estimated 711,000 in 1950.
Israel lost roughly 6,000 people, about one per cent of its Jewish population. Arab losses are less well documented.

effects_region.t: UN General Assembly Resolution 194 (December 1948) stated that refugees wishing to return to their homes and live at peace with their neighbours should be permitted to do so. The refugee question remains unresolved.

In the following two decades, several hundred thousand Jews left or were driven out of Arab countries, most of them settling in Israel. Claims over the property both groups left behind later became linked in negotiations.
Defeat discredited the Arab governments involved and contributed to political upheaval, including coups in Syria (1949) and Egypt (1952).

effects_world.t: Both the United States and the Soviet Union recognised Israel in May 1948. The conflict became one of the lasting international disputes of the Cold War era.

debates.q: Why did around 700,000 Palestinians leave their homes?

views.t: Morris, working from Israeli archives, argues that the exodus was mainly a product of the war itself: fear, the collapse of Palestinian society, and expulsions by Israeli forces in many places. He finds no single master plan for expulsion.
Walid Khalidi argues that the exodus was the result of a deliberate plan, pointing to the Haganah's Plan D (Plan Dalet) of March 1948.

Older official Israeli accounts said Arab leaders had urged the population to leave. Archival research since the 1980s found little evidence of a general call to leave, although local evacuations were ordered in some places.

debates.q: Was it a war of 'the few against the many'?

views.t: The traditional Israeli account presents a small, outnumbered Jewish community fighting the armies of several Arab states.

Revisionist historians ('new historians') argue that Israeli forces outnumbered the Arab expeditionary forces for much of the war, that the Arab coalition was divided, and that King Abdullah of Transjordan had a tacit understanding with the Zionist leadership.
Critics of the new historians, such as Efraim Karsh, dispute their use of sources and the 'collusion' thesis.

stories.title: The June 1967 war
stories.teaser: Six days that put the West Bank, Gaza, Sinai and the Golan under Israeli control.
stories.summary: In six days (5–10 June 1967) Israel defeated Egypt, Jordan and Syria. It took the Sinai Peninsula and Gaza Strip, the West Bank including East Jerusalem, and the Golan Heights. The occupation of these territories and the UN's 'land for peace' formula in Resolution 242 shaped the conflict for decades.

background.t: Tension rose in 1966–67 over raids by Palestinian guerrillas operating with Syrian support, Israeli reprisals, and clashes in the demilitarised zones along the Israeli–Syrian armistice line.
On 13 May 1967 the Soviet Union told Egypt that Israel was massing troops on the Syrian border. The report was false.

Egypt moved troops into Sinai, secured the withdrawal of the UN Emergency Force, and closed the Straits of Tiran to Israeli shipping. Israel had said since 1957 that it would treat such a closure as a cause for war. Jordan signed a defence pact with Egypt on 30 May.

course.t: On 5 June Israel launched a surprise air attack that destroyed most of the Egyptian air force on the ground, then advanced into Sinai and Gaza.
After Jordan opened fire, Israel captured East Jerusalem and the West Bank. On 9–10 June it took the Golan Heights from Syria. Ceasefires ended the fighting on 10 June.

outcome.t: Israel's losses were under 1,000 dead. Arab losses were many times higher, most of them Egyptian. Published estimates vary.
Several hundred thousand Palestinians fled or were expelled from the West Bank and Gaza, many of them refugees for the second time. Most of the Golan's Syrian population also left.

effects_region.t: UN Security Council Resolution 242 (22 November 1967) called for the withdrawal of Israeli armed forces from territories occupied in the conflict and for the right of every state in the area to live in peace within secure and recognised boundaries. It became the basis of the 'land for peace' formula.
The Arab League summit in Khartoum (August–September 1967) adopted a position of no peace with Israel, no recognition and no negotiations.

Israel extended its law and administration to an enlarged East Jerusalem and began building settlements in the occupied territories. The UN Security Council has repeatedly described the settlements as having no legal validity.
The defeat weakened Nasser and pan-Arab nationalism. Palestinian groups such as Fatah gained independence of action and took over the PLO by 1969.

effects_world.t: The Suez Canal stayed closed from 1967 until 1975. The Soviet Union broke off diplomatic relations with Israel, and the United States became Israel's main arms supplier.

debates.q: Why did the war break out?

views.t: Richard Parker argues that no side planned the war. He sees a chain of miscalculation: the false Soviet report, Nasser's escalation, and misjudged military balances.
Isabella Ginor and Gideon Remez argue that the Soviet Union deliberately provoked the crisis. Most historians regard this thesis as unproven.
Guy Laron stresses structural pressures: an arms race, economic crises, and the influence of the military in Israel, Egypt and Syria.

debates.q: Pre-emption or a war of choice?

views.t: Israel's government presented its attack as pre-emptive self-defence against an imminent threat. Michael Oren's account emphasises how threatened Israeli leaders and the public felt in May 1967.
Several contributors to the volume edited by Louis and Shlaim argue that Israeli leaders did not expect an imminent Egyptian attack and chose to strike while the military balance favoured them.

The English text calls for withdrawal 'from territories occupied', without the article 'the'. Israel has read this as not requiring withdrawal from all of them. Arab states and many others read it, together with the French text ('des territoires'), as requiring full withdrawal.

stories.title: The October 1973 war
stories.teaser: A surprise attack, an oil shock, and the road to the first Arab–Israeli peace treaty.
stories.summary: On 6 October 1973 Egypt and Syria attacked Israeli forces in Sinai and on the Golan Heights. After early Arab gains, Israel counter-attacked, crossing the Suez Canal and advancing towards Damascus before a UN ceasefire. The war ended without a clear military victory. It led to US-mediated disengagement, the Egypt–Israel peace treaty of 1979, and, through the Arab oil embargo, a global energy shock.

background.t: Egypt and Syria wanted to recover the territory lost in 1967. Diplomatic efforts stalled, and US–Soviet détente did not produce a settlement.
Israeli military intelligence held that Egypt would not go to war without the means to challenge Israeli air superiority. It discounted warning signs until hours before the attack.

course.t: The attack began on Yom Kippur, 6 October. Egyptian forces crossed the Suez Canal and broke through Israel's Bar-Lev Line. Syrian forces advanced on the Golan.
Both superpowers resupplied their partners by air. Israeli forces crossed the canal in mid-October and encircled the Egyptian Third Army.
UN Security Council Resolution 338 (22 October) called for a ceasefire. Fighting continued for several days, and a US–Soviet confrontation followed before the ceasefire held.

outcome.t: Both sides suffered heavy losses, with thousands killed.
UCDP records both the Israel–Egypt and the Israel–Syria fighting in 1973 at war level (1,000 or more battle deaths).
US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger mediated disengagement agreements with Egypt and Syria in 1974.

effects_region.t: Egypt and Israel signed the Camp David Accords in September 1978 and a peace treaty in March 1979. Israel withdrew from Sinai by April 1982. Egypt was suspended from the Arab League.
In Israel the surprise led to the Agranat Commission of inquiry and a lasting crisis of confidence in the political and military leadership.

effects_world.t: Arab oil producers cut output and embargoed the United States and other countries seen as supporting Israel. The price of oil rose from $2.90 a barrel before the embargo to $11.65 in January 1974.
The oil shock fed inflation in industrial economies that were already under inflationary pressure, and it changed the balance of power between oil producers and consumers.

debates.q: Why was Israel taken by surprise?

views.t: Uri Bar-Joseph attributes the surprise mainly to the rigid assumptions of Israel's military intelligence leadership and its handling of warnings, rather than to a lack of information.
Other accounts give more weight to Egyptian and Syrian deception and to political decisions not to mobilise or strike first.
Many scholars see the war as a limited operation, meant to break the diplomatic deadlock and draw the superpowers in rather than to reconquer all of Sinai by force.
Craig Daigle argues that US and Soviet priorities under détente had left the conflict unresolved and made war more likely.

stories.title: The Iran–Iraq war
stories.teaser: Eight years of war over a waterway, a revolution and regional power.

names.name: Qadisiyyat Saddam
names.used_by: Iraqi state usage under Saddam Hussein

stories.summary: Iraq invaded Iran on 22 September 1980. Iran had recaptured most of its territory by 1982 and carried the war into Iraq. Years of stalemate followed, along with attacks on cities and shipping and chemical warfare. A UN-brokered ceasefire took effect on 20 August 1988, with the border essentially unchanged.

background.t: The main territorial dispute concerned the Shatt al-Arab waterway. The 1975 Algiers agreement had set the border along its deepest channel.

After Iran's 1979 revolution, relations collapsed. Personal hostility between Saddam Hussein and Ayatollah Khomeini, ideological rivalry, and Iranian appeals to Iraq's Shi'a majority all played a part.
On 17 September 1980 Iraq abrogated the Algiers agreement. Five days later its forces crossed the border.

course.t: Iraq captured Khorramshahr in October 1980 but failed to take Abadan, and it went over to the defensive.
Iranian offensives in 1981–82 recovered Khorramshahr. In June 1982 Saddam announced a withdrawal, and in July Iran carried the war into Iraq. A long stalemate followed.
From 1983–84 both sides attacked each other's cities and Gulf shipping. In 1987 Kuwaiti tankers were placed under the US flag, and the US naval presence in the Gulf grew.
UN expert missions confirmed the use of chemical weapons. On 16 March 1988 Iraqi aircraft attacked the Kurdish town of Halabja with poison gas, killing at least 4,000 people, most of them civilians.

outcome.t: UN Security Council Resolution 598 (20 July 1987) demanded a ceasefire and withdrawal to internationally recognised borders. Iran accepted it in July 1988, and the ceasefire took effect on 20 August 1988 under UN observation.
Estimates of the human cost vary widely. Encyclopaedia Iranica, citing Dilip Hiro, gives about one million casualties (killed and wounded) and a cost of $1.19 trillion.

effects_region.t: Iraq ended the war heavily indebted, much of it to Gulf states. Scholars link these debts and disputes to Iraq's decision to invade Kuwait in 1990.
In Iran the war helped consolidate the revolutionary state and strengthened the Revolutionary Guards.

effects_world.t: The 'tanker war' drew outside powers into the Gulf: from 1987 the US Navy escorted reflagged Kuwaiti tankers.

views.t: One emphasis is opportunism: Iran's armed forces were weakened by post-revolutionary turmoil and the US arms cut-off, so Iraq saw a chance to win the Shatt al-Arab and regional leadership.
Another is defensive fear: Iraq's leadership worried about the Islamic Revolution spreading to Iraq's Shi'a majority. Murray and Woods, drawing on captured Iraqi records, show both motives at work.

debates.q: Did the United States give Iraq a 'green light'?

views.t: Some journalists and Iranian officials have claimed that Washington encouraged the invasion.
Hal Brands, using US and Iraqi archives, concludes that the claim is unfounded and that the Carter administration was surprised by the attack.

debates.q: How did the world respond to chemical weapons?

views.t: Joost Hiltermann argues that the United States and other governments muted criticism of Iraq's chemical attacks because they wanted to prevent an Iranian victory.
Early UN Security Council statements condemned the use of chemical weapons without naming Iraq.

notes.t: The border data (CShapes) draws these areas as part of Israel from June 1967, which reflects who controlled them. The striped area marks territory beyond the 1949 armistice line (the Green Line, dashed).
Sinai was returned to Egypt under the 1979 peace treaty; the withdrawal was completed in April 1982.
Israel extended its law to East Jerusalem and the Golan Heights. The UN Security Council declared both measures null and void.
The UN Security Council refers to the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, and Gaza as Palestinian territory occupied since 1967.
Iraq invaded Kuwait on 2 August 1990. The UN Security Council demanded an immediate withdrawal.
Iraq declared Kuwait annexed. The Security Council declared the annexation null and void.
A US-led coalition expelled Iraqi forces in February 1991.
